newsitem.title: UK: New Parkinson's drug makes old one work better.
newsitem.headline: New Parkinson's drug makes old one work better.

text.p: Drugs that help standard Parkinson's treatments work better may be the next line in treating patients with the debilitating brain illness, delegates told a conference on Monday.

Finnish drug leader Orion's Entacapone showed significant results with few side-effects when given with standard levodopa treatment, they told the 12th International Symposium on Parkinson's Disease in London.
Entacapone is a member of a class of drugs known as cathechol-O-methytransferase (COMT) inhibitors, which make more levodopa available in the body.
Levodopa, the standard Parkinson's treatment, only works well for about five years. After that it starts to wear off.

"This problem is clinically great because levodopa still today constitutes the core of therapy in Parkinson's disease," Dr Urpo Rinne, a neurologist at the University of Turku in Finland, told the conference.
Parkinson's, which causes tremors, progressive debilitation and sometimes dementia, is characterised by a lack of dopamine in the brain. Levodopa helps replenish it.
"COMT inhibition seems to be the next clinically significant improvement of levodopa treatment in Parkinson's disease," Rinne told the conference.
Dr Heikki Teravainen and colleagues at the University of Helsinki tested 15 patients and found entacapone improved clinical response.

Rinne's group, working with Orion, tested 21 Parkinson's patients and found entacapone increased availability of levodopa in the blood by 23 percent and improved response to the drug as measured by standard tests.
"For the time being, COMT inhibitors are one of the most important advances in the development of levodopa therapy for Parkinson patients," Rinne told the conference.
Parkinson's is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer's, afflicting about one percent of all people over 50.
